title: Before ranking runs, draw the noise: seed bands, bootstrap intervals and the error floor behind a percent error
summary: Two SciML figures ask whether differences between many training runs are real. One ranks all runs with confidence intervals and a seed-noise band; the other plots percent error against the size of the true value on log-log axes, where a fixed absolute error appears as a line of slope minus one.

media.alt: Log-scale scatter of one score for 115 runs ranked from best to worst, each a small coloured dot with a thin vertical interval, in three colours for three groups. A pale blue horizontal band lies under the best dots; the ranking rises slowly across the band and then sharply upward at the right.

source.caption: 115-run seed-noise floor — bootstrapped ranking
source.note: DISCLOSURE: these two figures show an internal objective (a composite error score on named species), a bootstrap setup and fitted slopes from an unpublished study. This explainer teaches only the generic reading; no scores, slopes, the noise-band factor or run categories are quoted.

read_the_figure.question: Which differences between runs exceed the noise, and what does a percent error mean for a quantity that is tiny?
read_the_figure.axes: Ranking figure: run number ranked best to worst (horizontal) against the score on a log axis (vertical); each dot has a bootstrap 95 percent interval over 80 test conditions, and the shaded band is the seed-to-seed noise around the best run. Scaling figure: true value (mass fraction, log) against absolute percent error (log), one colour per species, with fitted lines.
look_at: The shaded band: any run whose dot lies inside it cannot be told apart from the best run by this experiment. Count how many that is before reading the order.
The thin vertical lines: the bootstrap interval of the score over the test conditions. Overlapping intervals mean the order of those runs is not established.
The tail at the right: scores that are orders of magnitude worse. These runs failed; the log axis compresses them, so their spread is much larger than it looks.
Scaling figure: the fitted lines slope downward in log-log. A slope of minus one is the signature of a fixed absolute error: the percent error is that error divided by a shrinking true value.
Species far to the left (very small true values) have enormous percent errors, up to many orders of magnitude, even if their absolute error is negligible.
Legend entries give fitted slopes per species; here only the meaning of a slope is taught, not the values.
read_the_figure.proves: A rank list is only meaningful relative to its noise. A percent-error metric on small quantities mostly measures the floor of absolute error, not the quality of the model, so a trace species can look terrible while being as accurate as the main ones in absolute terms.
if_wrong: Top-ranked runs inside the noise band: the ranking among them is not supported; report them as a tie.
Intervals computed from a single seed: they ignore training noise.
Percent error used on quantities that approach zero: the metric is dominated by the denominator.
A fitted line through a cloud with large vertical scatter: the slope is a trend, not a law.
must_check: That the noise band is estimated from repeated runs with different seeds, and its width is stated.
That intervals are named (bootstrap over conditions, 95 percent) and resampled over the right unit.
That a log axis is used for scores that span decades.
That an absolute-error view accompanies any percent-error view of small quantities.

terms.meaning: The spread of a score when the same training recipe is repeated with different random seeds.
The smallest difference between two runs that the noise level would let you detect.
An interval from resampling the test conditions with replacement and recomputing the statistic.
Absolute error divided by the absolute true value, times 100.
A smallest error that does not scale with the quantity, from round-off, tolerances or output resolution.
A species present at very small mass fractions.

remember: A difference smaller than the seed noise is not a difference.
A bootstrap interval is only as good as the unit resampled; resample conditions, not individual time points.
log10 of percent error against log10 of the true value has slope -1 when the absolute error is fixed.
Report absolute and relative errors together for quantities that span many decades.
Fitted slopes on scattered log-log clouds are trends; report their uncertainty.

steps.title: Why a fixed absolute error gives slope minus one
steps.note: Take logs. The true value enters with a coefficient of -1, so on log-log axes the points of a species with a constant absolute error lie on a line of slope -1, shifted up or down by the size of epsilon.

steps.title: Reading the shaded band
steps.note: On a log axis the band is a fixed vertical width, because noise is multiplicative. The legend of the ranking states the band as a factor on the best run.

steps.title: Bootstrap over conditions
steps.tex: \hat s^{*}_b=\mathrm{median}\{e_{c}:c\in\mathcal C^{*}_b\},\quad \mathcal C^{*}_b\ \text{drawn with replacement from the 80 conditions}
steps.note: Repeat B times; the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the replicates form the 95 percent interval. It captures variation across test conditions but not across training seeds, which is why the seed band is drawn separately.

steps.title: Percent error turns tiny values into huge numbers
steps.note: The same absolute error gives errors differing by a factor 1e6. Hence the trace species at the left of the scaling figure.

worked.title: The same absolute error at two scales
worked.problem: A model has an absolute error of 1e-9 on every species. Compute the percent error for true values 1e-3 and 1e-7 and the slope on a log-log plot.
worked.answer: 1e-4 percent and 1 percent, slope -1: a pure absolute-error floor.

analyze.q: How many dots lie inside the shaded band, and what does that do to a statement such as 'run 1 is best'?
In the scaling figure, why do species with very small true values show percent errors above 100 percent even if the model is excellent in absolute terms?
Explain why the ranking figure draws two kinds of uncertainty (interval and band) and what each answers.

evaluate.q: A reader wants to choose the best of the 115 runs. What would you hand them instead of a rank?
evaluate.hint: A short list of statistical ties plus a rule.

evaluate.q: Would you use percent error to compare two models on a species at 1e-9? What metric would you use?
evaluate.hint: Absolute error, or error relative to a floor.

create: Redraw the ranking as a plot where runs inside the noise band are grouped, labelled as a tie, and the tail is shown on its own axis.
Design a metric for trace species that does not blow up as the true value tends to zero and say what it loses.

checks.q: What does the slope in the scaling figure tell you?
checks.answer: How the error changes with the size of the true value; a slope of -1 means a fixed absolute error.

checks.q: Absolute error 1e-8, true value 1e-5. Percent error?
Two runs have non-overlapping bootstrap intervals but sit inside the seed band. Which statement is supported?
checks.answer: That they differ on these test conditions, but a different training seed could reorder them: the difference is not shown to be a property of the recipe.

checks.q: Is a single score ranking across 115 runs enough to pick a recipe?
checks.hint: What if the best is inside the band?
checks.answer: No: report ties inside the band and look at other criteria such as cost, failure rate and absolute errors.

checks.q: Propose a better y axis for the scaling figure.
checks.answer: Plot absolute error against the true value, with the floor marked, or error scaled by a species-specific tolerance.
